title: Documentation RAG Pipeline
summary: A modular pipeline that retrieves web documentation and supplies it as context for generated answers.
problem: Answer technical questions using relevant documentation, with separate components for ingestion, retrieval, and generation.
approach: Load web pages and split documents into overlapping chunks.
Embed chunks with OpenAI, persist them in ChromaDB, and retrieve relevant context.
Compose retrieval and generation with LangChain; provide a separate RAGAS evaluation wrapper.

decisions.title: Separate pipeline stages
decisions.body: Document processing, vector storage, and answer generation live in separate classes, making their responsibilities visible.

decisions.title: Keep retrieval configurable
decisions.body: Chunk size and overlap are constructor parameters; retrieval defaults to four matches and accepts search settings.

decisions.title: Make evaluation explicit
decisions.body: A separate evaluator accepts questions, answers, contexts, and reference answers. Its presence does not establish answer quality.

limitations: The included tests cover chunking and processor defaults, not retrieval or answer quality.
The example runner does not yet invoke the evaluator; answer quality needs an end-to-end evaluation.
Answers are plain text without source citations. The prompt requests context-based answers but does not enforce grounding.

diagram.caption: The implemented ingestion-to-answer path; RAGAS evaluation is a separate component.

result: The repository brings document processing, persistent retrieval, and answer generation into one configurable pipeline. It also includes chunking tests and a separate evaluation wrapper.

title: Agentic Insight Analyst
summary: A feedback-analysis agent with model-selected tools, inspectable working memory, and explicit stopping rules.
problem: Turn survey scores and written feedback into a structured report while keeping tool choices and intermediate outputs inspectable.
approach: Inspect a CSV and ask a language model to propose analysis steps.
Select from registered tools for TF-IDF clustering, phrase extraction, score analysis, and simple summaries.
Record tool outputs in session memory, evaluate stopping conditions, and synthesize findings and recommendations.

decisions.title: Use a fixed tool registry
decisions.body: The controller validates selected tool names against a registry and prepares arguments in code.

decisions.title: Bound the analysis loop
decisions.body: Iteration limits, repeated-tool detection, and a heuristic progress score determine when analysis stops.

decisions.title: Expose intermediate work
decisions.body: Working memory records plans, tool selections, outputs, and evaluations; the API returns a structured report and execution trace.

limitations: Progress is estimated from insight counts, tool variety, and tool success; it does not verify the stated success criteria.
Summary and recommendation tools use word counts and templates; evaluating report usefulness is a separate next step.
Memory and background jobs are held in process. LLM failures can fall back to empty JSON without making the final success flag false.
The API accepts raw_text but does not pass it into the agent; the implemented analysis path uses CSV files.

diagram.caption: Tool selection repeats until a stopping rule fires, then the agent synthesizes a report.

result: The implementation connects an agent controller, a fixed set of analysis tools, session memory, and a FastAPI interface. Tests cover individual tools and a mocked agent flow.

title: Retail Demand Forecasting
summary: A forecasting workbench with data validation, temporal features, baseline and tree models, and evaluation utilities.
problem: Explore how retail sales history and calendar features can support demand forecasts, using a synthetic-data demonstration.
approach: Load and validate sales records, aggregate store-level demand, and split by date.
Create calendar, lag, rolling, and difference features for tree models alongside simple forecasting baselines.
Provide metric comparison, feature-importance inspection, model persistence, and separate MLflow logging utilities.

decisions.title: Keep simple baselines visible
decisions.body: Naive, seasonal-naive, and moving-average forecasts provide reference approaches alongside tree-based models.

decisions.title: Split observations by date
decisions.body: Train, validation, and test periods use chronological boundaries. Feature construction still needs correction to prevent target leakage.

decisions.title: Separate evaluation and tracking
decisions.body: Metric computation and MLflow logging have dedicated modules; the main runner initializes tracking but does not log complete training runs.

limitations: Rolling and difference features include the current sales target, leaking the answer into model inputs. Accuracy claims require corrected features and fresh evaluation.
The runner mixes daily-total baseline forecasts with store-level ML predictions, so comparisons and ensemble inputs need alignment.
The multi-step ML forecasting helper remains unimplemented. The demonstration uses synthetic data.

diagram.caption: Source-level training workflow; leakage and forecast alignment must be fixed before its scores are meaningful.

result: The workbench implements data validation, forecasting baselines, tree-model wrappers, and evaluation utilities. Correcting target leakage and aligning forecast granularity are necessary before comparing model scores.
